newsitem.title: HONG KONG: New Hong Kong chief justice faces tough challenge.
newsitem.headline: New Hong Kong chief justice faces tough challenge.

text.p: Hong Kong's newly-appointed chief judge faced a stiff challenge on Wednesday to establish a credible Court of Final Appeal before the handover to China now just weeks away.
Barrister Andrew Li, 48, scion of a prominent Hong Kong banking dynasty, got the post on Tuesday in a move likely to ease Western concern about civil liberties and independence of the judiciary.
Fellow lawyers and democracy camaigners say Li, who has never been a judge, is a highly-regarded legalist and independent-minded. "He's no puppet", said a colleague.
He now faces a race against time that will require all his diplomatic and political skills as well as legal expertise.
Li was named to the post of Chief Justice of Hong Kong's yet-to-be-established Court of Final Appeal by future leader Tung Chee-hwa on Tuesday.
"The main problem is that time is running short and he has a number of major tasks on hand," Audrey Eu, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Bar Association, said on Wednesday.
"Probably the most pressing one to consider ... is the setting up of the Court of Final Appeal."

Some critics have painted a doomsday picture of Hong Kong's chances of maintaining legal freedoms and rule of law after the handover of the community of 6.4 million to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.
They fret about Chinese-style cronyism creeping in, leading to an exodus of top judges and point to Tung's plans to dilute civil liberties laws as the thin edge of a wedge.
But all sides of Hong Kong's political spectrum have put aside their differences to hail Li, a Cambridge-educated Hong Kongh Chinese barrister chosen from a list of about 140 candidates.
"He is the best man for the delicate task ahead, not merely to defend legal independence but being seen to defend it," said one associate.

Li, a member of the colonial executive council, the British governor's inner cabinet, is regarded as a legal heavyweight, shrewd and tough enough to resist any political meddling, politicians and lawyers say.

Britain and China had once envisaged establishing the Court of Final Appeal (CFA) to replace the London-based Privy Council as final legal arbiter for Hong Kong well ahead of the handover to allow time to settle to its task.
But Sino-British hostility over the mild democratic reforms introduced by the last colonial governor Chris Patten in the early and mid-1990s scuppered that plan.
The upshot is that Hong Kong's judiciary faces a six-week period of musical chairs as Li selects the legal brains to run the CFA and then fills the slots vacated by his promotions.

The Court of Final Appeal will consist of three permanent judges plus one non-resident judge drawn from another Commonwealth country which still practises the English common law system, due to continue in Hong Kong after the handover.
The 1984 Joint Declaration in which Britain agreed to return its colony also binds China to maintaining Hong Kong's separate legal, political and social way of life unchanged for 50 years.
Promotions will inevitably create gaps in the ranks of the senior judiciary, already thinned by retirements ahead of the handover, legal sources said.
"Mr Li must persuade those of the highest calibre not to retire early," said the Hong Kong Standard newspaper.

He also has to find means of wooing Hong Kong's top legal brains from lucrative private practice to sit on the bench, filling gaps that could damage the efficiency of the already backlogged court system.
"For a top QC (Queen's Counsel or senior advocate), becoming a judge is like taking a vow of poverty," a senior member of the Hong Kong government legal department said.

On a less controversial note, Li will have to decide whether to dispense with the wigs and gowns of the British legal system and whether to continue with addressing High Court judges as "My Lord", a term redolent of colonialism.
